intro.html: Some things are plain to see; others only seem true; and some are understood without anyone saying a word. Careful readers notice which is which, because writers use these words to tell you how much to trust a claim.

Plain to see: manifest, patent, unmistakable, palpable (you can almost touch it), overt (done in the open). Plain and shameless: blatant, flagrant. Only seeming: ostensible, purported. Unspoken: tacit.
When a passage says the ostensible reason or the purported letter, the writer is warning you: this is what was claimed, not necessarily what is true.

words.def: clear and plain to see or understand
words.ex: Her joy was {manifest} in the way she skipped all the way home.
words.ctx: Though he said nothing, Gus’s disappointment was {manifest}: his shoulders slumped, his smile vanished and he left the party early.
words.etym: From Latin manifestus, “caught in the act, plain to see.”
words.note: As a verb, manifest means to show plainly: her worry manifested itself in sleepless nights.

mn.text: Pip swears he never touched the paint, but his hands and nose are bright blue; his guilt is {manifest}.

scene.alt: A boy with paint dripping from his hands insists he did not spill the blue paint as his mother points at him.

words.def: so strong or clear that it can almost be touched
words.ex: The tension in the room was {palpable} as the judges opened the envelope.
words.ctx: As the last runner neared the finish line, the excitement in the stadium was {palpable}; strangers grabbed one another’s arms, and no one could sit still.
words.etym: From Late Latin palpabilis, “able to be touched,” from palpare (to touch gently, to stroke).

mn.cue: PALP-ABLE: you could almost PAT it
mn.text: As the spelling bee reaches its last word, the nerves in the room are so thick that you could almost reach out and pat them; the tension is {palpable}.

scene.alt: Three nervous students at a spelling bee tremble; one reaches out as if the tension could be touched.

words.def: done or shown openly, not hidden
words.ex: Lila’s {overt} yawning during the long speech made the speaker frown.
words.ctx: Unlike the sly hints her brother dropped, Ivy’s request was {overt}: she taped a picture of the bike she wanted right on the refrigerator door.
words.etym: From Old French overt, “opened,” from ovrir (to open).

mn.cue: OVER-T: right out in the OPEN
mn.text: Ivy does not drop hints; she hangs a giant sign over the fridge that says “I WANT A BIKE!” Her wish is {overt}.

scene.alt: A girl points proudly at a huge banner that says she wants a bike, as her father laughs.

words.def: completely obvious and done without shame
words.ex: Copying your neighbor’s answers word for word is {blatant} cheating.
words.ctx: Jonah’s excuse was a {blatant} lie; he claimed he had been home all evening, but half the class had seen him at the arcade.

mn.cue: BLAT-ant: as loud as a BLARING horn
mn.text: Rex copies Pip’s test while reading the answers out loud, as loud as a blaring horn; cheating that shameless and obvious is {blatant}.

scene.alt: A teen leans over a boy’s test and loudly reads the answers, cheating without hiding it.

words.ex: Picking up the soccer ball and running it into the goal was a {flagrant} break of the rules.
words.ctx: Parking across three spaces in front of the hospital entrance was a {flagrant} violation, and the driver came back to find a ticket on his windshield.
words.etym: From Latin flagrans, “burning, blazing,” from flagrare (to burn).
words.note: Flagrant (shockingly obvious) is not fragrant (sweet-smelling). Flagrant suggests a wrong that blazes; blatant suggests one done without shame.

mn.cue: FLAG + RANT: a wrong that BLAZES
mn.text: Rex picks up the soccer ball and carries it into the goal; the referee waves her red flag and rants. A foul that glaringly wrong is {flagrant}.

scene.alt: A player runs off carrying the soccer ball in his hands while an angry referee waves a red flag.

words.ex: His story about a dog eating his homework was a {patent} fib; he doesn’t even have a dog.
words.ctx: The claim that the old bridge was safe was {patent} nonsense: anyone could see the cracks running through its stone arches.
words.etym: From Latin patens, “lying open,” from patere (to be open).
words.note: As a noun, a patent is the legal right to an invention. The adjective is most often met in the adverb patently: a patently false claim.

mn.cue: PAT’S TENT: as plain as can be
mn.text: Pat pitches a bright orange tent in the middle of the lawn and calls it her secret hideout; that hiding place is {patent} to everyone.

scene.alt: A girl named Pat waves from a big orange tent she calls a secret hideout while a boy laughs and points.

words.def: stated or seeming to be true, but perhaps not the real thing
words.ex: The {ostensible} reason for his visit was to return a book, but he stayed for three helpings of pie.
words.ctx: Her {ostensible} purpose in calling was to ask about homework, but it soon became clear that she really wanted to know who was going to the dance.
words.etym: From Latin ostendere, “to show, to hold out for view”: the ostensible reason is the one held up for show.

mn.text: Dev says he is visiting Nana Lou to fix her clock, which sounds sensible, but his eyes are on her cookies; fixing the clock is his {ostensible} reason.

scene.alt: A teen with a toolbox says he came to fix his grandmother’s clock, but he is really eyeing her cookies.

words.def: claimed or said to be, but not proven
words.ex: The museum showed a {purported} dinosaur egg that turned out to be a smooth river stone.
words.ctx: The {purported} treasure map was a fake; experts showed that its “ancient” paper was only a few years old.
words.etym: From purport, from Old French purporter, “to carry, to convey”: pur- (forth) + porter (to carry).

mn.text: The seller swears his purring cat once belonged to a king, but he has no proof at all; it is only the {purported} royal cat.

scene.alt: A seller claims his purring cat in a tiny crown belonged to a king, while a doubtful teen asks for proof.

words.def: understood without being said out loud
words.ex: With a {tacit} nod, the twins agreed to keep the surprise party a secret.
words.ctx: No one ever announced the rule, but there was a {tacit} agreement in the house: whoever cooked dinner did not have to wash the dishes.
words.etym: From Latin tacitus, “silent,” from tacere (to be silent). Taciturn comes from the same root.

mn.cue: TAC = SILENT: a deal with no words
mn.text: Across the dinner table, Zoe winks and Kai nods; without a word, they agree to swap peas for carrots. Their deal is {tacit}.

scene.alt: Two children wink at each other across a table, agreeing without a word.

words.def: impossible to mistake for anything else; very clear
words.ex: The {unmistakable} smell of fresh bread drifted down the street from the bakery.
words.ctx: Even in the crowded station, Grandpa’s laugh was {unmistakable}; we simply followed the booming sound and found him by the ticket window.

mn.cue: UN-MISTAKE-ABLE: a giraffe in a crowd
mn.text: Grandpa brings his pet giraffe to the busy station; in a crowd of a hundred people, no one could mistake where he is. The giraffe is {unmistakable}.

scene.alt: A grandfather waves from a crowded station beside his very tall pet giraffe.

what it tells you
tone

claimed or seeming, maybe not true

after.html: Flagrant (from Latin for blazing) is not fragrant (sweet-smelling). And when you see ostensibly, expect a twist: “Ostensibly, he came to help; in fact, he came to eat.”

items.q: Which word means shockingly obvious and wrong?
items.why: Flagrant means glaringly wrong. Fragrant means sweet-smelling.

items.q: “The ostensible purpose of the meeting was to plan the picnic.” The writer hints that…
choices: the real purpose may have been something else
items.why: Ostensible means stated or seeming. Writers use it to hint that the real reason was different.

items.q: A tacit agreement is one that is…
items.why: Tacit comes from Latin for silent: the agreement is understood, never spoken.

items.q: True or false: overt and covert are opposites.
items.why: True. Overt means done openly; covert means done in secret.
